summary: Adds a variance procedure to IETF process rules, an escape for situations where existing procedures are not working or do not seem to apply. It is a Best Current Practice, now historic, and was replaced by RFC 2026.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1871 describes how the IETF can make a public exception when its written standards procedures do not fit or cause deadlock. It was marked Historic and later replaced by RFC 2026.

questions: what is the ietf variance procedure
how can ietf bypass its normal procedures
when can the iesg grant a variance
how can people appeal a variance
subtitle: A public procedure for handling cases where IETF rules do not work

tldr.problem: IETF procedures can reach a deadlock or fail to give guidance for a situation.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG may grant a narrowly limited exception after a working group or ad hoc committee recommends it, public review occurs, and the benefits are judged to outweigh the costs.
tldr.outcome: This historic procedure was later replaced by RFC 2026.

today: RFC 1871 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 2026.

sections.title: When a Variance May Be Needed
sections.content:
The RFC adds an interim variance procedure to the IETF rules in RFC 1602 and RFC 1603. It is for cases where following the written procedures creates a deadlock or where the procedures provide no guidance.

A variance allows a specification to enter or advance on the standards track despite not meeting some requirements in Section 5 of RFC 1602. The RFC requires a public process with an opportunity for concerned parties to comment.
sections.plainLanguage: A variance is an exception for a case where the existing IETF rules block progress or do not apply. The exception must be considered publicly, with a chance for people to comment.

sections.title: The Review and Decision
sections.content:
The responsible IETF Working Group, or an ad hoc committee if there is no working group, may bring the issue to the IESG. The IESG proposes a solution and must decide whether likely benefits to the Internet community outweigh the costs of not meeting the usual requirements.

The IESG considers technical merit, whether the process goals can be reached without an exception, alternatives, wider effects and precedent, and whether the exception can be kept narrow. It documents the proposal in an Internet-Draft and calls an extended Last Call for public review. The IESG accepts or revises the proposal after considering comments; the IAB hears and decides appeals.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG proposes and evaluates the exception after a responsible group raises the problem. It must weigh benefits against costs, invite public comments, and keep any exception as narrow as possible; the IAB handles appeals.

sections.title: Limits and Status
sections.content:
The IESG may limit a variance to particular parts of the requirements and add restrictions to protect the Internet community. The proposed solution may address one specific case or set a procedure for similar cases.

The RFC states that it modifies RFC 1602 and RFC 1603. It also says that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: An exception can cover only selected requirements and can include extra limits. The RFC does not discuss security issues.

references.text: IAB and IESG, "Internet Standards Process -- Revision 2," RFC 1602, March 1994.
